segments.say: Lesson 2. Clients, Servers, A P Is & Databases 101. What actually happens between your phone and a backend: I P addresses, ports, H T T P requests and responses, jason, A P Is and where data is stored.

Almost every app works the same way: a client (phone app, browser) sends a request over the internet to a server, which runs code, reads or writes a database, and sends back a response. Here is an analogy. A restaurant: you (the client) give your order to a waiter using the menu (the A P I). The kitchen (the server) cooks using ingredients from the storeroom (the database), and the waiter brings back your plate (the response).

Why does this matter? Every system design question assumes you know this vocabulary cold. A P Is and databases appear in every single design. A few key words. Client: The app or browser that sends requests. Server: A computer that runs backend code and answers requests. I P address: A machine's address on the network, for example 142.250.1.1. Port: A numbered "door" on a machine for a specific service (443 equals H T T P S). H T T P: The language clients and servers use for requests and responses. A P I: The set of U R Ls and rules a server offers to clients. jason: The common text format for data: "name": "Karthik". Database: Software that stores data permanently and lets you query it.

segments.sec: Watch: One request, start to finish
segments.say: One request, start to finish. You open your profile in an app. The app needs your data from the company's computers.

segments.sec: Watch: One request, start to finish
segments.say: It sends an H T T P request over the internet to the server's I P address (34.12.8.9) on port 443 (the standard H T T P S door).

segments.sec: Watch: One request, start to finish
segments.say: The server is just a computer (usually in a cloud data centre) running your backend code. It checks who you are and what you asked for.

segments.sec: Watch: One request, start to finish
segments.say: It queries the database: "give me user 42's profile". The database finds the row and returns it.

segments.sec: Watch: One request, start to finish
segments.say: The server sends back an H T T P response with status 200 OK and your data as jason. The app renders it. Usually all in under ~200 ms.

segments.sec: Watch: Inside an HTTP request and response
segments.say: Inside an H T T P request and response. A request starts with a method (G E T equals read) and a path (which resource).

segments.sec: Watch: Inside an HTTP request and response
segments.say: Headers carry extra info: which site, who you are (an auth token), what format you want back.

segments.sec: Watch: Inside an HTTP request and response
segments.say: For creating or updating (P O S T/P U T), the request also has a body, usually jason.

segments.sec: Watch: Inside an HTTP request and response
segments.say: The response has a status code (200 OK, 404 Not Found, 500 Server Error), headers and a body. Simple text going back and forth.
What an A P I is. Many different clients need the same data and actions.
An A P I (Application Programming Interface) is the menu your server offers: the exact requests it accepts and what each returns. Clients don't touch the database directly.
Each item is an endpoint: a method plus path. A rest A P I uses nouns for resources (/users, /orders) and H T T P methods for actions (G E T read, P O S T create, P U T update, DELETE remove).

segments.sec: Watch: How a database stores data
segments.say: How a database stores data. A relational database stores data in tables: columns are fields (id, name, city) and rows are records.

segments.sec: Watch: How a database stores data
segments.say: The primary key (id) uniquely identifies each row. Other tables point to it (orders.user id leads to users.id).

segments.sec: Watch: How a database stores data
segments.say: You ask for data with a query. The database finds and returns the matching row. Later lessons cover indexes (making this fast) and sequel versus no sequel.

H T T P methods and status codes (must know). G E T read, P O S T create, P U T/P A T C H update, DELETE remove. 2xx success (200 OK, 201 Created), 3xx redirect, 4xx client mistake (400 bad request, 401 not logged in, 403 forbidden, 404 not found, 429 too many requests), 5xx server failure (500, 503).
A tiny backend, so it feels real (Python / FastAPI). Here is the code. Pause the video to read it line by line.

Networking in 4 lines. I P address: which machine. Port: which program on it (80 H T T P, 443 H T T P S, 5432 Postgres). D N S turns names into I Ps. T C P: reliable, ordered delivery (web, A P Is). U D P: fast, no guarantees (video calls, games). H T T P S equals H T T P encrypted with T L S.
Stateless servers. Each request carries everything the server needs (like an auth token), so any server copy can handle any request. This one idea is what makes scaling out easy (Scaling lesson).

Say it in the interview. "Clients call our rest A P I over H T T P S. Stateless app servers authenticate the request, read or write the database, and return jason with the right status code. Because the servers are stateless, we can run many of them behind a load balancer.".
Let's compare. Delivery: guaranteed, in order, best effort. Speed: slightly slower (handshakes, retries), faster. Used for: web, A P Is, databases, email, video calls, gaming, D N S.

Who does what. Client: asks, phone app, browser. A P I: defines what can be asked, G E T /users/42. Server: runs logic, Python FastAPI, Java Spring. Database: stores data permanently, Postgres, MongoDB.

A likely interview question: Walk me through what happens when an app loads your profile. A strong answer: The client sends an H T T P S G E T to the A P I endpoint (D N S gives the server's I P). A stateless server authenticates the token, queries the database by the user's primary key, and returns 200 with jason, which the app renders.
That's it for Clients, Servers, A P Is & Databases 101. Now play the quiz and games in the app to lock it in. See you in the next lesson.
